question: What type of energy does an ultrasound machine use to create images inside the body?
explanation: Ultrasound uses safe, high-frequency sound waves that bounce off your tissues to form a picture, meaning there's no radiation involved at all!

question: Why do doctors and nurses prefer ultrasound when a patient needs repeated scans over a short time?

options.A: it does not use harmful ionizing radiation
options.B: It is totally painless and needs no practice
options.C: It gives a much clearer view of bones than a CT scan
options.D: It completely replaces the need for blood tests

explanation: Because it lacks harmful radiation, ultrasound is super safe and can be repeated as many times as needed to monitor healing.

question: Why do we apply that slippery water-based gel to a patient's skin before doing an ultrasound?

options.A: To get rid of air pockets that block sound waves
options.B: To cool down the hot scanner probe
options.C: To numb the skin so the scan doesn't hurt
options.D: To leave a mark on the skin for later

explanation: Sound waves struggle to travel through air. The gel acts like a bridge, helping the waves glide smoothly into the body.

question: How do hard structures like bones usually look on a standard ultrasound image?

options.A: As glowing green areas showing high activity
options.B: They block the sound and leave a dark shadow behind them
options.D: As bright white lines that let sound pass right through

explanation: Bone bounces most of the sound back, preventing the waves from going deeper—this creates what we call an acoustic shadow behind it.

question: Which type of ultrasound is best when you need to check how fast and in what direction blood is flowing?
explanation: Doppler is your go-to scan for blood vessels because it specifically tracks moving red blood cells to measure flow.

question: What does a regular B-Mode ultrasound show you on the screen?

options.A: A bright color map of bone strength
options.B: A two-dimensional greyscale picture of internal organs
options.C: A live wave graph of the heart's electrical rhythm
options.D: A 3D heat map of the body's temperature

explanation: Think of B-Mode as your standard black-and-white anatomical view that outlines the shape and structure of organs.

question: Which of these common health issues is an abdominal ultrasound usually ordered to check?

options.C: A broken bone in the lower leg

explanation: Ultrasound is brilliant at looking inside fluid-filled organs like the gallbladder to spot stones or blockages.

question: A patient comes in with a suspected blood clot in their leg vein (deep vein thrombosis). What scan will the doctor likely order?
explanation: A vascular Doppler scan is specifically designed to peek inside blood vessels and catch clots early.

question: Why is a patient scheduled for an abdominal ultrasound usually told to fast (no food or water) for a few hours beforehand?

options.A: To keep their blood pressure steady before the scan
options.B: To cut down on tummy gas and keep the gallbladder full
options.C: To make sure they have an empty bladder for a pelvic check
options.D: To stop them from throwing up during the procedure

explanation: Food creates gas that blocks sound waves, and fasting keeps the gallbladder nice and full so it's easy to see!

question: Why are patients told to drink water and hold their urine before a pelvic ultrasound?

options.A: A full bladder pushes pelvic organs up into a better viewing position
options.B: To encourage bowel movements before the scan
options.C: A full bladder is needed to turn on the color Doppler
options.D: To stop them from getting dehydrated during the test

explanation: A distended bladder acts like a clear window, pushing gas-out of the way and giving a fantastic view of pelvic structures.

question: As a nurse assisting with an ultrasound-guided needle procedure, what is your most important duty?

options.A: Adjusting the machine's sound frequency during the scan
options.B: Keeping the area strictly sterile and helping the patient stay still
options.D: Reading and writing the final report

explanation: Invasive bedside procedures need strict infection control and a steady patient to keep everything safe and accurate.

question: Why might a nurse position an abdominal ultrasound patient to lie on their left side?

options.A: To stop them from rolling off the bed
options.B: To shift bowel gas away from the organs being checked
options.C: To boost their blood pressure for the Doppler scan
options.D: To relax their tummy muscles completely

explanation: Shifting the patient's position helps move pesky gas-filled loops of the bowel out of the way of the ultrasound beam.

question: What is an immediate nursing task to take care of right after an ultrasound scan ends?

options.A: Send the ultrasound machine back to central sterilization
options.B: Flush the IV line with heparin
options.C: Check the patient's blood sugar every hour
options.D: Wipe away any leftover coupling gel from the patient's skin

explanation: Cleaning up the sticky gel shows good bedside manner and keeps the patient comfortable and clean.

question: Which of these is NOT something a nurse should do after an invasive ultrasound-guided procedure?

options.A: Check the patient's vital signs to make sure they are stable
options.B: Document the finished procedure in the patient chart
options.C: Give the family the final medical diagnosis
options.D: Watch the puncture site for bleeding or swelling

explanation: Nurses monitor recovery and report vital signs, but giving the final medical diagnosis is strictly the doctor's or radiologist's job.

question: What is the biggest perk of using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in emergency or acute care?

options.A: It gives instant answers right at the bedside to guide fast care
options.B: It requires no training for hospital staff to use
options.C: It replaces every single blood test in the emergency room
options.D: It offers higher picture quality than giant hospital machines

explanation: POCUS is designed to be quick and portable, giving clinicians immediate answers right when every second counts.

question: A post-surgical patient cannot pass urine and you suspect they are retaining urine. What is the best bedside tool to check?
explanation: A portable bladder scanner is quick, non-invasive, and tells you right away how much urine is trapped in the bladder.
